For each flagged item, rule whether the key's answer is uniquely defensible from the evidence (key-uniquely-defensible), whether two answers are defensible (ambiguous), or whether the key is wrong (key-wrong). 3	Answer semantics:
4	- hypothesis: "supported" = the evidence, taken together, supports the claim more than its rivals; "contradicted" = the evidence counts against it; "unknown" = the evidence does not discriminate, so the claim is live but unestablished.
5	- edge (a claimed link from one condition to another): "causal" = the evidence supports a causal link (for example temporal order plus mechanism plus covariation with the main rival ruled out, a natural experiment, or an intervention result); "association-only" = they co-occur or correlate in the evidence but causation is not established; "contradicted" = evidence counts against the link; "unknown" = evidence is insufficient even to show association.
6	- action: "preferred" = among the best next actions given the evidence; "acceptable" = reasonable but not among the best; "premature" = could be right if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed, but committing now is not justified; "harmful" = likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party, or disable a protective control.
7	- sufficiency (item SUFF): is the evidence sufficient to commit to the action you rank highest, where that action is substantive rather than merely evidence-gathering? "sufficient" or "insufficient". Concluding that no intervention is warranted counts as a substantive decision.
8	- Items with asOfStage set must be answered using only evidence whose stage is at or before that stage.

368	CASE OD2-HO-NOCONC-2 (NOCONC, technical): ratequote's 5xx rate ticks up in the week of a release
369	Setting: Brindlemoor Freight runs an internal pricing service called ratequote. It returns shipping quotes to the customer booking web app, to the partner-sync integration jobs and to internal reporting. It handles about 2.1 million requests a week behind an internal load balancer and is owned by the Pricing Platform team. The team's error metric is the share of requests that return an HTTP 5xx status. Over 24 pods, the service reads from a quote cache and falls back to a read replica of the pricing database. It also calls an upstream tariff-rates service owned by another team.
370	Presenting request: On Tuesday 3 November 2026 the Director of Platform Engineering asked two questions: did release v4.18 cause last week's rise in ratequote's 5xx rate, and should it be rolled back today? You are asked what, if anything, explains the rise and what the team should do.
371	INITIAL EVIDENCE
372	E1 [stage S1] Email from Marguerite Osei-Lund, Director of Platform Engineering, to the Pricing Platform team, Tue 3 Nov 2026 (leadership-account): Subject: ratequote errors. 'ratequote's 5xx rate went from 0.31% to 0.41% last week. That is a 34% jump, and it happened right after v4.18 shipped on Tuesday. Dario's rollout numbers show the new pods erroring at almost twice the rate of the old ones, so I think we know what happened. I want v4.18 rolled back today. Someone in the channel also suggested muting all of ratequote's 5xx alerting, burn-rate page included, for a month until things settle. I'm open to that if the noise is distracting people.'
373	E2 [stage S1] Export of dashboard 'ratequote / errors', default four-week view, taken Mon 2 Nov (telemetry): Source: internal load balancer access logs. Weekly 5xx rate, weeks starting Monday: 5 Oct 0.29%; 12 Oct 0.32%; 19 Oct 0.31% (6,410 of 2,086,000 requests); 26 Oct 0.41% (8,690 of 2,112,000). Request volume in the week of 26 Oct was 1.2% above the prior week. Seven-day error-budget burn: 0.82x. Note added by SRE Fen Achterberg: 'I recounted 5xx lines directly from the raw load balancer log files for both weeks and got 6,402 and 8,677. The small gaps are late-shipped log batches. Nobody has edited the dashboard query since March.'
374	E3 [stage S1] Release record RQ-4.18, filed by release engineer Dario Kestrel (change-record): Deployed Tue 27 Oct as a rolling update. Started 14:10, completed 15:02 with all 24 pods on v4.18. Contents: HTTP client library fetchwell bumped from 5.2 to 5.4; new optional 'surcharge_breakdown' response field behind a flag (flag off); removal of the unused /v1/legacy-quote endpoint. Rollout observation (my note): 'During the rollout I compared 5xx on v4.18 pods with v4.17 pods. v4.18: 0.52% (31 of 5,960 requests). v4.17: 0.30% (22 of 7,330). Same minutes, same traffic. That looks like the new version to me, and my guess is the fetchwell bump.'
375	E4 [stage S1] Change calendar, ratequote and dependencies, 26 Oct–1 Nov (change-record): Tue 27 Oct 14:10: ratequote v4.18 (RQ-4.18). Wed 28 Oct 09:30: ratequote's read replica moved from host class m-std to host class m-dense (DB-2291). The previous hosts are kept until 20 Nov as a fallback. No load balancer, gateway or dashboard changes recorded. Not on the calendar: partner-sync's month-end reconciliation. The partner-sync team runs it 'around the last two business days of the month', which would be Thu 29–Fri 30 Oct this month, and it normally accounts for about 18% of ratequote requests. Partner-sync has not confirmed when it ran this time.
376	E5 [stage S1] Pricing Platform service-level policy, revision 4 (January 2026), extract (document): Objective: 99.5% of ratequote requests succeed in each calendar month, giving an error budget of 0.5%. Paging: the burn-rate page fires when the 7-day budget burn exceeds 2x. A warning ticket opens when the 1-hour 5xx rate exceeds 0.6%. Weekly review: a week's 5xx rate is investigated as an incident if it lies above the upper edge of the normal band (the mean plus two standard deviations of the preceding 26 weekly rates), or if the burn-rate page fired. Otherwise the week is noted at ops review and no action is taken.
377	E6 [stage S1] Booking analytics and client SDK metrics, weeks of 19 and 26 Oct (system-record): Quote-to-booking completion in the customer web app was 41.0% in the week of 19 Oct and 41.2% in the week of 26 Oct. The ratequote client SDK used by the web app and by partner-sync retries once on any 5xx after 200 ms. Retry success was 98.7% and 98.6% for the two weeks. Requests still failing after retry: 83 and 122. Customer support logged no quote-related complaints in either week.
378	CATALOGUE (full contents)
379	C1 [stage S1] Code diff summary, ratequote v4.17 → v4.18 - Source repository, compare view, summarised by the Pricing Platform tech lead (change-record): 47 files changed. fetchwell 5.2 → 5.4 is a lock-file change only. ratequote still sets its own connect timeout (300 ms) and read timeout (800 ms) explicitly in config, unchanged. 'surcharge_breakdown' adds new serializer code that runs only when flag quote.surcharge_breakdown is on; the flag was off for all callers from 27 Oct to 1 Nov. The /v1/legacy-quote handler was deleted; gateway logs show no calls to it since July. Two log messages were reworded. Nothing changed in the cache, database access or retry code.
380	C2 [stage S1] ratequote application error log, 5xx counts by class, 19 Oct–1 Nov - Application log aggregation, query run by SRE on 3 Nov (log): Counts for 19–25 Oct → 26 Oct–1 Nov. 504 timeout (request exceeded 800 ms): 4,530 → 6,480. 503 shed under load: 610 → 700. 500 unhandled exception: 1,262 → 1,497; the top signatures in both weeks are 'TariffNotFound race' and 'NullCurrencyCode', both present since spring. 502 bad gateway: 8 → 13. No exception signature appears in the second week that is missing from the first. A 504 is logged the same way whether the slow call went to the read replica or to the tariff-rates service, so the log cannot tell them apart.

Read latency p50 stayed at 4–5 ms throughout. Read latency p99 by week: 28 Sep 39 ms; 5 Oct 35; 12 Oct 37; 19 Oct 36; week of 26 Oct 41 (38 before the move, 42 after). Replication lag stayed under 1 s throughout. Peak CPU was 46% on the old hosts and 39% on the new ones. Connection errors: none. DBA comment: 'Over the summer, p99 on the old hosts ranged from 33 to 44 ms by week. The new class should be faster, but I can't tell from this whether it is.'
382	C4 [stage S1] Interview with partner-sync team lead - Interview notes, Ilse Marrow, partner-sync lead, 3 Nov (staff-account): 'Month-end reconciliation re-quotes every open partner shipment, so it puts heavy load on ratequote for a few hours. The week of 26 Oct really was higher than the week before (0.31% to 0.41%), and the raw-log recount in E2 and the query history in C7 rule out a counting artefact. 'Within ordinary variation' (C6) means the rise needs no special cause. It does not undo the fact that the two events happened in the same week, so the 'association is debatable' objection does not fit the stated definition. Nothing counts against the link: C1, C2 and C14 do not exclude a fetchwell effect, and C8 supplies an untested mechanism. So contradicted is out. Causal is also out, because C10 explains the only isolating comparison as warm-up seen in every rollout, and the replica move and partner traffic are confounded with the release. The key also stays consistent with R5, which is keyed unknown because there co-occurrence itself is unestablished (C4). Association-only is the single answer the definitions support.
rulings.fix: No change needed. Optionally, the edge definition could say explicitly that a single same-period co-occurrence counts as association even when the size of the change is within normal variation.

rulings.explanation: The reasoning is the same as for R1. The replica moved on Wed 28 Oct, inside the week whose rate really was higher (E2, E4), so co-occurrence is shown. C3 adds a little covariation: replica p99 went from 38 ms before the move to 42 ms after, though still within the summer's range. Nothing counts against the link. C3 shows no errors and no lag, but the log cannot tell replica 504s from tariff-rates 504s (C2), so contradicted is not supported. Nothing establishes causation. Association-only follows directly from the stated definition, and unknown would require that co-occurrence was not shown, which is not the case here.

Opening an incident and assigning an engineer is an evidence-gathering step, not a fix that depends on one hypothesis. It causes no harm: it does not suppress information, disable a control or punish anyone. It is also not among the best actions. Policy reserves incidents for weeks outside the band or weeks where the burn-rate page fired (E5). The week is in band (C6), three earlier similar investigations found nothing (C6), and the comparison that would settle the version question (same-age pods on different versions) does not exist in last week's data (C10). That makes it a low-yield but reasonable response to the Director's doubt, which is what acceptable means. Premature is defined as an action that would be right if an unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed but that commits too early. That fits commitments such as a rollback (A1) or moving the replica back (A4), but it fits a look-back investigation poorly: confirming H1 would call for a fix, not for this investigation. Premature is a stretch, so acceptable is the uniquely best fit.
rulings.fix: No change needed. To close off the premature reading completely, the action definitions could state that non-committal investigation steps are graded preferred, acceptable or harmful, and that premature is reserved for actions that commit to a hypothesis.

rulings.explanation: Contradicted would need evidence that counts against H1. What C10 does is remove E3's support: the new-pod excess shows up in every rollout, including a config-only redeploy. Taking away the evidence for a claim is not the same as evidence against it. The rest of the record leaves a plausible path open. C8 shows that fetchwell 5.3 cut the idle-eviction default from 90 s to 30 s, untested, on the tariff-rates call path. 504s, which cannot be attributed to a source (C2), make up most of the week's increase (+1,950 of +2,280). C1 shows that timeouts and the cache, database and retry code are unchanged, but it does not cover library defaults. C14 is not comparable. H3 (within normal variation) being supported does not exclude H1 either, because a small real effect is also consistent with an in-band week. The evidence does not discriminate, so H1 is live but unestablished, which is the definition of unknown.

Harmful means likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party or disable a protective control. Rolling back does none of these to any meaningful degree. It takes about 50 minutes, nothing callers depend on is in v4.18 (C1, C5), and the warm-up cost is about 10–20 errors that the 98.6% SDK retry success largely absorbs (C10, E6). That is negligible against a weekly volume of about 2.1M requests. A rollback would even give some information about H1. It would be the right fix if H1 were confirmed, but H1 is unknown: the comparison behind it is confounded by warm-up (C10) and the week is in band (C6). That is exactly the premature definition. The point that it 'acts on a confounded comparison' is an argument for premature, not for harmful.
